newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook - Gasoline flat despite stocks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook - Gasoline flat despite stocks.

text.p: U.S. Gulf and New York Harbor gasoline differentials should continue to languish at low levels in the coming week despite some concerns about low stock levels and the relatively strong U.S. demand.
"There's more potential for a pop than a fall back (differentials), but I expect it to stay about flat for the next couple of weeks," one gasoline broker said.

Seasonal gasoline bulls are poised to drive prices higher, though there has been no evidence that spot market traders are ready to snap up barrels, with offers at both New York Harbor and the U.S. Gul seen as plentiful.
"The only place it's performing strongly is on the screen," another gasoline player said, adding that those NYMEX gasoline gains were largely tied to heavy crack spread buying.
NYMEX April gasoline has gained about five cents in the past week, rebounding from its low at 61.20 cents to Monday's peak at 66.30 cents.
"But spot gasoline is still sloppy in New York. You just can't sell it," he added.

U.S. gasoline inventories sat at 201.820 million barrels in the latest American Petroleum Institute report, about 10.3 million barrels below the year-ago levels. In addition, implied demand figures were surprisingly high at 7.9 million barrels a day for the latest reporting week and 8.1 million barrels a day in the previous week.
Weaker MTBE (methyl tertiary butyl ether) prices may keep reformulated gasoline prices from surging upward, one market player said.
Ample supply and tight storage space in the East Coast continued to pressure the MTBE market last week, extending its drop from 86.50 cents on Jan. 16 to 76.25 cents on Friday.
Heating oil continued to languish at its lowest prices since June 1996, with outright New York Harbor quoted at about 54.00 cents.

Weak demand because of this winter's above-normal temperatures in the U.S. Northeast, the key demand market, thwarted players who bet on higher prices late last fall. And most market watchers expect no major rebound in either differentials or futures prices in the coming weeks.
In the Midwest U.S., the focus is also expected to be on gasoline, with a continued selloff on Chicago winter-grade material likely to exert downward pressure on differentials.
The switch from winter- to summer-grade (from nine-pound-square-inch Reid vapor pressure material from 13.5-pound) is slated for the end of the month.

"People are dumping it, nobody's interested in winter stuff," one Chicago trader said, pegging conventional unleaded at 9.00 cents below the April print at midday Monday -- a half cent weaker than Friday diffs.
"It's very weak," the trader said, adding the differential is usually about 2.25 cents below the print this time of year.

But increasing agricultural demand for diesel is expected to help differentials. "Demand is kicking in, they're starting to get into their fields," one Midwest trader, adding that diffs firmed about 0.25 cent Monday from Friday levels.

At the West Coast, gasoline stocks also remain tight, with supplies down 587,000 barrels as of February 28 with half-a-dozen of the region's refiners entering or still in maintenance, costing the region about 300,000 bpd in refining capacity.

But traders said refineries shut in January could begin start-up next week, including the crude unit at Mobil's 130,000 bpd crude Torrance, Calif., refinery and half the unit's at Exxon's 130,000 bpd plant near San Francisco.
"Mobil should be back soon, next week," a trader said.
-- New York Energy Desk + 1 212 859 1620
